description: The Two Pointers technique uses two (or three) indices moving through a data structure to collapse nested-loop O(n^2) scans into a single O(n) pass. Pointers may converge from both ends, travel in the same direction at different speeds, walk two separate arrays, or expand outward from a center. The unifying idea is a monotonic decision rule that tells you which pointer to move without ever backtracking.
important_details: Pre-condition: the input must be sorted, or possess a monotonic property that makes the 'which pointer moves' decision deterministic.
Opposite Direction: pointers start at 0 and n-1 and converge; move based on comparison against a target.
Same Direction: a slow pointer marks the boundary of the valid/processed region while a fast pointer scans ahead — used for in-place O(1)-space modification.
Two Arrays: independent pointers over two sorted inputs, advancing whichever is lagging.
Expand from Center: a pointer pair grows outward from every possible center — the standard O(n^2) palindrome technique.
Critical invariant: no pointer ever moves backward. If your solution requires backtracking a pointer, it is not a two-pointer solution.
other_relevant_details: Always ask whether sorting the input first unlocks two pointers, even when the problem never says 'sorted' — an O(n log n) sort plus an O(n) scan beats an O(n^2) brute force. Also watch for problems where two pointers replaces a HashMap: it trades O(n) space for O(1) space, which is often the actual follow-up question in an interview.

variations.description: Start pointers at both ends of a sorted array and move them toward the center based on how the current pair compares to a target condition (sum, area, capacity).
important_details: Requires the array to be sorted, or sortable without losing information you need (e.g. original indices).
At each step exactly one pointer moves, chosen by comparing the current pair's value to the target.
Correctness argument: when sum < target, no pair using the current left can be better, so left is safely discarded — this greedy elimination is why O(n) is sufficient.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) for the scan, O(n log n) if a sort is required. Space: O(1).

problems.name: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted

variations.description: Generalizes two-sum to triplets, quadruplets, and beyond by sorting the array, fixing k-2 outer loop indices, and running a converging two-pointer scan on the remaining suffix.
important_details: 3Sum = sort + one outer loop + inner two-pointer, giving O(n^2) instead of O(n^3); 4Sum adds another outer loop for O(n^3).
Duplicate skipping is the number one source of wrong answers: after fixing an outer value, skip identical adjacent values; after finding a valid pair, advance both pointers past their duplicates.
Early-exit pruning matters for OA time limits: if the smallest possible remaining sum exceeds the target, break out of the outer loop entirely.
For 'closest' variants, track the best absolute difference rather than searching for an exact match.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n^(k-1)) for k-Sum. Space: O(1) excluding the output and sort overhead.

variations.description: A slow pointer tracks the write position for the valid portion of the array while a fast pointer scans ahead reading candidates, enabling in-place filtering and de-duplication with O(1) space.
important_details: Slow only advances when a keeper element is written; fast always advances.
The returned length is the slow index (or slow+1 depending on whether slow points at the last written slot or the next free slot — pick one convention and stay consistent).
For the 'allow at most k duplicates' generalization, compare nums[fast] against nums[slow - k] instead of nums[slow].
Elements past the returned length are allowed to be garbage in most problem statements — do not waste time clearing them.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) — the key advantage over building a new array or using a HashSet.

problems.name: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II

variations.description: Independent pointers traverse two separate sorted sequences at once, advancing whichever is behind, to merge, intersect, or compare them in a single linear pass.
important_details: Both inputs must be sorted, or become sorted during the algorithm (as in merge sort's merge step).
Merging into a fixed-size first array is done from the BACK to avoid overwriting unread elements — a classic interview gotcha.
After the main loop, flush whatever remains in the longer sequence.
For subsequence checking, only one pointer conditionally advances (the pattern pointer moves only on a match) — a degenerate but very common case.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(m + n). Space: O(1) when merging in-place from the back.

problems.name: Longest Word in Dictionary through Deleting

variations.description: A three-pointer variant (low, mid, high) that partitions an array into three regions in a single pass — famously for sorting 0s, 1s, and 2s, and as the partition step of three-way quicksort.
important_details: low marks the end of the 0-region, high marks the start of the 2-region, mid is the scanner.
When swapping with high, do NOT advance mid — the value swapped in has not been examined yet. When swapping with low, advance both.
Loop condition is mid <= high, not mid < high — getting this wrong silently drops the last element.
Generalizes to partitioning around any pivot value, which is the core of quickselect for Kth-element problems.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) single pass. Space: O(1).

problems.name: Partition Array According to Given Pivot

variations.description: For each of the 2n-1 possible centers (n single characters plus n-1 gaps between characters), grow a pointer pair outward while the palindrome condition holds.
important_details: You must handle both odd-length centers (a single index) and even-length centers (a gap between two indices) — forgetting even centers is the classic bug.
Each expansion is O(n) and there are O(n) centers, giving O(n^2) total — acceptable for n up to a few thousand.
For counting palindromic substrings, each successful expansion step contributes exactly one substring to the count.
Manacher's algorithm solves the same problem in O(n) but is rarely required; know that it exists and mention it as the optimal follow-up.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n^2). Space: O(1) — beats the O(n^2)-space interval DP solution for the same problem.

problems.name: Longest Palindrome by Concatenating Two Letter Words

variations.description: Converging or parallel pointers over one or two strings to validate palindromes, compare after applying edits (backspaces, deletions), or check character-level structural properties, all in O(1) space.
important_details: Skip non-alphanumeric characters inline rather than pre-building a cleaned string — that is what keeps space at O(1).
For 'valid palindrome with at most one deletion', on the first mismatch branch into two checks: skip the left character, or skip the right character.
Backspace-comparison problems are best solved by scanning from the RIGHT, maintaining a skip counter, since a backspace affects what came before it.
Case-folding and Unicode assumptions should be clarified with the interviewer before coding.

variations.description: Combines converging pointers with running maxima or precomputed prefix/suffix arrays so each step's decision uses aggregate information about everything seen so far from each side.
important_details: Trapping Rain Water is the canonical case: maintain leftMax and rightMax, and always process the side with the smaller max, because that side's answer is already fully determined.
The insight is that if leftMax < rightMax, water above the left pointer depends only on leftMax — the taller right wall is guaranteed to exist.
This converts an O(n)-space prefix/suffix-array solution into an O(1)-space two-pointer solution, which is the standard follow-up.
The same restructuring applies to any problem where a prefix array and a suffix array are consumed in opposite directions.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1), down from O(n) for the prefix/suffix-array version.

variations.description: Uses the Lomuto or Hoare partition scheme — itself a two-pointer routine — to place a pivot in its final sorted position, then recurses into only one side to find the Kth smallest/largest in expected O(n).
important_details: Partitioning is a two-pointer sweep: one pointer scans, the other marks the boundary of the 'less than pivot' region.
After partitioning, compare the pivot's final index to k to decide which half to recurse into — you discard the other half entirely, which is why it is O(n) expected rather than O(n log n).
Worst case is O(n^2) on adversarial input; randomizing the pivot choice makes that vanishingly unlikely and is expected in interviews.
Compare against the heap approach (O(n log k), O(k) space) — quickselect wins on time, heaps win when data streams in or k is tiny.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n) expected, O(n^2) worst case. Space: O(1) iterative.

problems.name: Kth Largest Element in an Array
